design_decisions.reason: The sourced requirement is specifically about competition ENTRY, not about owning or flying a CCC wing recreationally. A pilot who organised a survey of nearly 300 two-liner owners treats under about 20 hours on your previous wing as a warning sign before a two-liner specifically — and has a real case attached: someone who moved onto one with around 11 hours, took a severe collapse in rough terrain, and threw their reserve. More hours on the wing you're on now, flown properly rather than just logged, is what closes this.

gates.message: This is the one skill two experts who disagree about almost everything else agree matters before a two-liner — and this class's narrower, tapered tips raise cravat risk further still. Fewer lines give collapsing fabric more room to tangle, and clearing one isn't the same instinct as clearing an ordinary collapse. Practised, deliberately, over water or with a coach, is what this needs.

source.cites: Lobb and Janaway both name cravat clearing.

gates.message: This is the other skill both experts agree on. A two-liner hands you pitch movement sooner and wants a lighter touch than the wing you're on — catching a surge on the brakes, holding it on the rear risers while you're on bar, easing off before it dives. Worth building deliberately rather than meeting for the first time on the new wing.

source.cites: Pitch control named by both Lobb and Janaway.

gates.message: Managing the energy that comes out of a frontal collapse is on the short list of things one detailed analysis expects before a two-liner. Worth meeting deliberately, with height or over water, rather than for the first time on the new wing.

source.cites: Malin Lobb names frontal-collapse energy management as a must-have SIV skill.

gates.message: In a survey of nearly 300 pilots flying two-line C wings, about a quarter had real difficulty getting ears in on the shorter line set — and the survey names it as one of its specific warning signs. Worth being confident with ears on the wing you're on before relying on them on a new one with a different pull.

source.cites: Lindenstruth's survey.

gates.message: A survey of two-liner pilots names leaning on the bar passively, without working the brakes as the wing accelerates, as a specific warning sign — it gives a feeling of security rather than actual control, on exactly the wings where that control matters most. Easing the bar on while watching the pitch, and trimming the pressure as you go, is the habit worth building first.

source.cites: Lindenstruth's red-flag list.

gates.message: By your own account, your current wing hasn't yet been the thing stopping you — and that's the clearest marker this ladder's research gives, more pointedly here than anywhere below. Seb Ospina describes his own early jump to high-performance wings as something that set his progression back rather than forward. A later wing is very unlikely to change that on its own. Usually it means there's performance still sitting in the wing you've got, waiting to be collected.

Why the change, what you expect it to give you, and how decisions get made on a day you're unsure about are where this result comes from — and none of that is a judgement on you as a pilot. It usually takes a conversation rather than another fifty hours in the air.

always_output.instructor_recommendation: Whatever this says, talk it through with an instructor or, better still, someone who has actually competed or coached at CCC level. That matters more here than anywhere else on the ladder: this is the step with the least independent criteria to check a result against, and a competition mentor can tell you things no questionnaire can — including whether the specific wing suits the kind of flying or racing you actually want to do.
always_output.disclaimer: This is a self-assessment tool based on published guidance from national associations, manufacturers, retailers and instructors. It isn't an instructor, it can't see you fly, and it isn't a safety clearance. Wing choice is your responsibility and your instructor's advice always comes first.
always_output.methodology_note: This is the thinnest-evidenced step on the whole ladder, and worth saying so plainly rather than dressing up a thin result as a precise one. CCC isn't a safety class — it's a competition equipment specification — and almost nothing published addresses pilot readiness for it specifically, beyond what already applies to a well-flown EN-D. What IS well documented is how pilots actually get into CCC-eligible competition: through a recognised advanced or competition rating, not a wing-specific skills test. So this step leans on that rating question more than any other on the ladder, and carries the skills and judgement questions from the step below largely unchanged, because nothing suggests they stop mattering — not because new evidence demands a stricter version of them. Every weight and gate links back to the criterion it came from.
